inline.s: [Plank-carrying fellow] A term of the Chan grove. It originally refers to a laborer who carries a plank of wood on his back, able to see only straight ahead but not to left or right; therefore the Chan gate uses it as a metaphor for one whose view is one-sided and cannot penetrate the whole. Here it refers to those who take a little as enough in their Chan practice, who attain “returning to the one” and deem it final, mistaking the phantom city for the treasure-place. This clinging to “returning to the one” is like carrying a plank on the back, seeing only one side and not the whole. Thus the song says:
“What a pity you sit on the pure ground
(stagnating in the state of returning to the one)
, and will not let it go, taking it as extraordinary, not knowing it has instead become a hindrance to the Dharma.” “I urge you, my friend, do not carry the plank
(do not cling to the state of returning to the one)

[Phantom city] A conjured city. From the parable of the phantom city in the Lotus Sutra. The parable of the phantom city tells of how the attainment of buddhahood by all sentient beings is the treasure-place, but the road to that treasure-place is arduous and long. The Buddha, fearing the travelers would grow weary and turn back, conjured up a city along the way, so that they might rest, gather their strength, and then press on to the treasure-place. Wishing to enable all sentient beings to realize the fruit of buddhahood, yet because sentient beings are timid and weak and cannot bear it, he first spoke of the nirvana of the Lesser Vehicle, so that having attained this nirvana they might rest for a while, and from there arouse the great resolve and advance toward the true treasure-place of the great nirvana (the fruit of buddhahood) of the Greater Vehicle. (For the commentary, see
The Commentary on the Song of the Plank-Carrying Fellow
